#### 17. `WahwahProcessor` (`wah`), `BassAndTrebleProcessor` (`basstreble`), and `NotchFilterProcessor` (`notch`) — Parameter Logic Traps (`BUG-23`, `BUG-24`, `BUG-29`)
* **Locations**:
  * `WahwahProcessor.java` (lines 62–65):
    ```java
    @Override
    public boolean isAudible() {
        return isEnabled() && depth.getCurrentRaw() > 0;
    }
    ```
    If the user sets `wah_depth` (`LFO Depth`) to `0%` in order to use **Auto-Wah** (`wah_auto > 0%`, envelope follower mode) or a static resonant filter (`wah_offset`), `isAudible()` returns `false` and `FxRackChain` completely bypasses `WahwahProcessor`!
  * `BassAndTrebleProcessor.java` (lines 67–79) & `StudioFragment.java` (lines 1766–1768, 2180–2182):
    When `link` (`Link Bass/Treble`) is enabled and both `bass` and `treble` are `0.0 dB`, `buildSections()` forces `b = 3.0; t = 3.0;` (`+3.0 dB` boost on both bands), and `StudioFragment` overwrites the user's `0.0 dB` knob values with `+3.0 dB`. Setting `0.0 dB` with `Link` enabled is impossible.
  * `NotchFilterProcessor.java` (lines 65–76):
    When `preset` (`Quick Pick`) is `1` (`50 Hz hum`) or `2` (`60 Hz hum`), `buildSections()` hardcodes `f = 50.0` or `60.0` and ignores `freq.getFloat()`.

#### 18. `LoudnessNormalizationProcessor` (`loudness`) — Early Return Skips `True-Peak Ceiling` (`loud_ceiling`) and Soft-Clip Exceeds Ceiling by Up to `+6 dB` (`BUG-25`)
* **Location**: `app/src/main/java/com/example/audiorecorder/fx/LoudnessNormalizationProcessor.java` (lines 193–215)
* **Affected Parameters**: `loud_ceiling` (`True-Peak Ceiling`, `-9.0..0.0 dB`, default `-1.0 dB`), `loud_target` (`Target Loudness`)
* **Root Causes**:
  1. **Early return skips ceiling**:
     ```java
     float gain = Dsp.dbToLin(gainDb);
     if (gain == 1f) return; // <-- Returns before applying loud_ceiling!
     ```
     If the audio is already at the target LUFS/RMS (`appliedGainDb == 0f`), `processInPlace()` returns at line 202 and **never executes the `loud_ceiling` limiter loop** (lines 206–215), leaving peaks above `loud_ceiling` untouched!
  2. **Soft-clip formula exceeds `ceilLin` instead of bounding at `ceilLin`**:
     Line 212 computes `float s = ceilLin + over / (1f + over / ceilLin);`. When `a > ceilLin` (`over = a - ceilLin > 0`), `s` is strictly **greater** than `ceilLin` (approaching `2 * ceilLin`, or `+6 dB` above `loud_ceiling`)! A true ceiling must never exceed `ceilLin`.

#### 19. `SpectralNoiseReductionProcessor` (`specnr`) & `SpectralEditProcessor` (`spectraledit`) — Per-Chunk STFT Re-Instantiation & `Spectral Delete` Gain Inversion (`BUG-26`)
* **Locations**:
  * `SpectralNoiseReductionProcessor.java` (lines 166–220)
  * `SpectralEditProcessor.java` (lines 71–103)
  * `StftProcessor.java` (lines 68–107)
* **Root Causes**:
  1. **Stateless chunked STFT**: Both processors allocate a new `StftProcessor(FFT_SIZE, HOP_SIZE)` on every `processInPlace` call (`1024` frames in live playback, `4096` frames in offline bake). Because `StftProcessor.process()` pads each chunk with zeros on both sides without carrying overlap-add buffers across calls, any spectral modification creates time-aliased circular-convolution tails that are abruptly cut off at every 1024/4096-sample boundary (`46.8 Hz` / `11.7 Hz` frame-rate modulation).
  2. **`SpectralEditProcessor` (`se_mode == 2`, `"Spectral Delete / Notch"`)**:
     Line 93: `float targetDb = modeIdx == 2 ? (Math.abs(g) > 0.1f ? -Math.abs(g) : -24f) : g;`. At default `se_gain = 0.0 dB`, `"Spectral Delete / Notch"` only attenuates by `-24 dB` (not a full notch), and moving `se_gain` to `-1.0 dB` or `+1.0 dB` **weakens** the notch from `-24 dB` to `-1 dB`!
  3. **Brickwall Gaussian truncation in `Spectral Parametric EQ` (`se_mode == 0`)**:
     At `hz = f1` and `hz = f2`, `d = ±0.5`, so `weight = exp(-0.25) = 0.7788`, which is abruptly zeroed outside `[f1, f2]`, creating sharp spectral steps at `f1` and `f2`.

#### 20. `PlosiveBreathSuppressorProcessor` (`plosive`), `DeEsserProcessor` (`deesssplit`), `ProCompressorProcessor` (`comp`), & `MultibandCompressorProcessor` (`mbcomp`) (`BUG-27`, `BUG-28`)
* **Locations & Root Causes**:
  * **`PlosiveBreathSuppressorProcessor.java` (lines 99–103)**: `plosive_breath` (`Breath Attenuation`) never measures high-frequency breath energy, scales the user's dB setting by `0.45f` max, and keeps `breathWeight >= 0.15f` even during loud speech (`midDb > -12 dBFS`), permanently attenuating the entire full-band signal by `0.0675 * plosive_breath` dB!
  * **`DeEsserProcessor.java` (lines 71–116)**: Subtracts a 2nd-order Butterworth low-pass (`splitLow`) from the dry input (`high = buf - lowBand`). Because a 2nd-order Butterworth LP has a `-90°` phase shift at `ds_freq`, `1 - LP(s)` is **not** a complementary high-pass filter — it has a `+3 dB` resonant peak near `ds_freq` and leaks phase-shifted low frequencies into the "high" band. It also has no attack/release parameters, ramping linearly over 64 samples (`1.33 ms`).
  * **`ProCompressorProcessor.java` (lines 136–157)**:
    * Scales `(ratio - 1)` by `amount = amt.getCurrentRaw() / 100f` (`effRatio = 1f + (ratio - 1f) * amount`), so the user's `comp_ratio` (`Ratio`) setting is silently weakened whenever `Compression % < 100%`.
    * Applies static makeup gain `makeupDb = -threshDb * slope * 0.5f` immediately on initial silence (`gainCur` ramps from `1.0` to `fastDbToLin(makeupDb)` in the first 16 samples before any voice arrives).
  * **`MultibandCompressorProcessor.java` (lines 171–173)**: Hardcodes `rms = false` in `envLow.detect`, `envMid.detect`, and `envHigh.detect`, and clamps `hx = Math.max(lx + 50f, highXover.getCurrentRaw())` internally without syncing the UI parameter when `mb_lowx >= mb_highx - 50`.

### Part 3: Pipeline, Save-Time Bake, Sub-Selection, Multi-Instance & Preview Bugs

#### 21. `ConversionJobs.dispatchSave()` Drops All 9 Stage 7 Offline / Time / Duration Effects on Save (`BUG-02`)
* **Location**: `app/src/main/java/com/example/audiorecorder/ConversionJobs.java` (lines 572–589, 621–636)
* **Affected Effects**: `tempo`, `speedpitch`, `changepitch`, `slidestretch`, `paulstretch`, `fade`, `timeline`, `truncsil`, `generator`
* **Root Cause**:
  When `needsFxBake` is `true` at save time, `ConversionJobs.dispatchSave()` creates `DspChain chain = new DspChain(info.channels, cfg)` and calls `EditEngine.applyDspToRange(raw, 0, totalFrames, chain, null)`.
  * `EditEngine.applyDspToRange` only calls `chain.processInPlace(...)` -> `FxRackChain.processInPlace(...)`.
  * `FxRackChain.processInPlace()` (line 266) has `if (!p.isEnabled() || p.isOfflineOnly()) continue;`!
  * Unlike `StudioFragment.commitDspFx()`, `ConversionJobs.dispatchSave()` **never checks `chain.offlineProcessors()` and never calls `EditEngine.applyLengthChangingEffectToRange()`**!
* **Impact**: Any unbaked offline/time effect in the rack is **100% skipped and absent from the saved file**.

---

#### 22. `StudioFragment.runSaveDispatch()` + `resetFxRackAfterApply()` Destroys Sub-Selection FX Bakes and Re-Bakes Over the Full File (`BUG-03`)
* **Location**: `app/src/main/java/com/example/audiorecorder/StudioFragment.java` (lines 1104–1117, 1791–1797, 2497–2531)
* **Root Cause**:
  1. When the user selects a sub-range `[fxApplyTargetStart, fxApplyTargetEnd)` and commits FX (pressing Stop in FX mode), `commitDspFx()` bakes the effect into the sub-selection of `currentRawFile`, sets `dspBakedToRaw = true; dspSubRangeBaked = true;`, and calls `resetFxRackAfterApply()`.
  2. Despite the comment in `commitDspFx()` stating `"the raw file and waveform now carry the processed audio, so start a fresh, blank rack"`, `resetFxRackAfterApply()` **leaves all `dspConfig.slots` enabled (`dspConfig.isActive() == true`)**!
  3. If the user subsequently touches any FX knob (or toggles a slot), `onSlotMutated` sets `lastEditWasSubRangeBake = true; dspBakedToRaw = false;`.
  4. When the user saves (`runSaveDispatch()`, lines 1104–1117), it sees `lastEditWasSubRangeBake && dspConfig.isActive()`, **pops the undo stack** (discarding the sub-range bake!), marks `needsFxBake = true`, and passes `dspConfig` to `ConversionJobs.dispatchSave()`, which bakes the rack across **`[0, totalFrames)` (the entire recording)** instead of the user's sub-selection!

---

#### 23. `DspChain` Multi-Instance Legacy Stage Overwrite & `ProToneProcessor` Split vs. Unsplit Wet/Dry Mismatch (`BUG-22`)
* **Location**: `app/src/main/java/com/example/audiorecorder/DspChain.java` (lines 382–442, 672–778) and `ProToneProcessor.java` (lines 111–201)
* **Root Causes**:
  1. **Duplicate legacy stage primary `value` overwrite**:
     `Config.addOrFocusSlot()` appends duplicate `EffectSlot`s even for the 8 legacy stages. In `DspChain.ensureRackSlots()`, the first legacy slot binds to the canonical processor (`instanceKey == null`) and the second binds to a new instance (`instanceKey = "slot:..."`). However, `Config.syncLegacyFieldsFromSlots()` iterates over `slots` and overwrites `cfg.compPct` (and `noisePct`, `deEssPct`, `hpfCutoffHz`, `warmthPct`, `presencePct`, `gatePct`, `limiterPct`) with the **last** enabled slot's value! Then `rack.applyLegacyConfig(cfg)` writes that last slot's value into the **first** canonical processor (`instanceKey == null`), so both instances run with the 2nd slot's primary value!
  2. **`ProToneProcessor` (`Warmth` / `Presence`) wet/dry mix scales dB instead of linear sample mix**:
     `ProToneProcessor.handlesOwnWetDryMix()` returns `true` whenever `warmthSlotMix < 0.999f || presenceSlotMix < 0.999f`. Instead of mixing dry and wet audio linearly (`(1 - mix) * dry + mix * wet`), `updateTargets()` multiplies the shelf filter's **dB gain** by `wMix` and `pMix` (`9f * wMix` dB), producing a completely different frequency/phase response from linear wet/dry mixing (and differing from `processWarmthOnly` / `processPresenceOnly` when the two stages are separated in the rack!).

---

#### 24. `RawFloatPlayer` — Live Preview Playhead & Pause/Resume Broken on Time-Stretched Audio (`BUG-15`)
* **Location**: `app/src/main/java/com/example/audiorecorder/RawFloatPlayer.java` (lines 201–215, 302–342)
* **Root Cause**:
  When playing an offline-rendered buffer `offlineBuf` whose length `outFrames` differs from the source selection `limitFrame - startFramePos`:
  ```java
  public long positionFrames() {
      ...
      long head = track.getPlaybackHeadPosition() & 0xFFFFFFFFL;
      long limit = stopAtFrame > 0 ? stopAtFrame : totalFrames;
      return Math.min(limit, startFramePos + head);
  }
  ```
  `head` advances in **stretched output frames** (`0..outFrames`), whereas `limit` (`stopAtFrame`) is in **unstretched source frames** (`limitFrame`).
  * When an effect stretches audio longer (`outFrames > limitFrame - startFramePos`, e.g. `Change Tempo -50%`, `Paulstretch`, `Timeline Repeat`), `startFramePos + head` hits `limit` partway through playback: the UI playhead freezes at the end of the selection while audio keeps playing, and pressing **Pause** records `framePos = limitFrame`, losing the playback position!
  * When an effect shortens audio (`outFrames < limitFrame - startFramePos`, e.g. `Change Tempo +100%`, `Truncate Silence`), `startFramePos + head` stops short of `limitFrame` and jumps at playback completion.

---

#### 25. `EditEngine.applyLengthChangingEffectToRange` — Zero-Crossing Snap Drops/Duplicates Up to 240 Frames & Misreports `newTotal` (`BUG-16`)
* **Location**: `app/src/main/java/com/example/audiorecorder/EditEngine.java` (lines 460–517, 672–720)
* **Root Cause**:
  1. Line 470 reads the selected region `[startFrame, endFrame)` using the exact `endFrame`.
  2. Line 494 calls `saveTailFrom(raw, endFrame, tailTmp)`, which calls `Dsp.snapToZeroCrossing(..., endFrame, ..., 240)` and shifts the tail start by up to `±240 frames` (`±5 ms`), either duplicating or deleting up to 240 frames at `endFrame`!
  3. Line 502 calls `spliceTailAfterReplace(raw, startFrame + newFrames, tailTmp)`, which overlaps the first `fade` (`240`) frames of `tailTmp` over the last `240` frames of `rendered` (`replaceEndFrame - fade`), making the actual file length `startFrame + newFrames + tailFrames - fade`.
  4. Line 505 returns `long newTotal = startFrame + newFrames + tailFrames;` (off by `+fade` frames), which `StudioFragment.commitDspFx()` uses to compute `regionEnd` for the next offline processor in the chain!

---

#### 26. Double Wet/Dry Mixing (`BUG-30`) & `TeleValue` Keyboard Step Bypass / `FxPreviewPeaks` Flag (`BUG-31`)
* **Double Wet/Dry Mix (`BUG-30`)**:
  `FreeverbReverbProcessor` (`rv_wet`, `rv_dry`, `rv_wetonly`), `PhaserProcessor` (`ph_mix`), `ChorusFlangerProcessor` (`ch_mix`), and `VocoderProcessor` (`vc_orig`) each have internal dry/wet mix controls, while `handlesOwnWetDryMix()` returns `false` (default in `AudioProcessor`). Adjusting the rack slot's `Wet-Dry Mix` blends the dry input a second time on top of the already-mixed output.
* **`TeleValue.commitTyped()` Bypasses `FxParameter.step` (`BUG-31a`)**:
  In `TeleValue.java` (lines 483–505), double-tap keyboard entry parses `Double.parseDouble(raw) * valueScale` and calls `setValue(v, true)`, which clamps to `[min, max]` without rounding to `FxParameter.step` (`clampRaw`), allowing off-grid raw integer values.
* **`FxPreviewPeaks.renderRegionInternal()` Marks Non-Length-Changing Offline Effects as `lengthChanged = true` (`BUG-31b`)**:
  In `FxPreviewPeaks.java` (line 224), `isLiveTimeline` returns `new LiveRegionResult(..., true, newTotalFrames, ...)` unconditionally whenever `!chain.offlineProcessors().isEmpty()`, even for `FadeProcessor`, `ChangePitchProcessor`, and `TimelineUtilityProcessor` (Invert/Reverse) where `rFrames == dryFrames`.

## Prioritized Remediation Roadmap

1. **Immediate Data-Safety Fixes (P0)**:
   * **`EditEngine.flushTailIntoRange`**: Fix `raf.readFully(Dsp.toBytes(dry, ...))` by reading into a `byte[]` and converting via `Dsp.toFloats`, and mix decaying tail energy additively onto `dry` rather than overwriting post-selection audio with the full FX chain.
   * **`ConversionJobs.dispatchSave`**: Execute offline processors (`chain.offlineProcessors()` via `EditEngine.applyLengthChangingEffectToRange`) before `EditEngine.applyDspToRange` whenever `needsFxBake` is true.
   * **`StudioFragment.commitDspFx` / `resetFxRackAfterApply`**: Either clear/disable baked slots upon commit or persist the sub-selection range `[fxApplyTargetStart, fxApplyTargetEnd)` so save-time re-bakes never expand a sub-selection bake to `[0, totalFrames)`.
   * **`ClickRemovalProcessor` & `RepairProcessor`**: Remove the `!any` comb-filter branch in `ClickRemovalProcessor` and the `!repairedAny` fallback LPC branch in `RepairProcessor` so clean audio is never corrupted; fix `halfWin = Math.max(1, maxSpike / 2)` in `ClickRemovalProcessor`.
2. **Time & Envelope Semantics Fixes (P1)**:
   * **`BrickwallLimiterProcessor` & `ProLimiterProcessor`**: Remove `bufPeak * 0.72f` / `bufMax * 0.65f` adaptive thresholds so limiters only act near `Ceiling`; read the `peakRing` lookahead buffer; hold `gainDb` constant while `holdCounter > 0`; remove `ballisticsTrimDb` and `0.65f` input-gain scaling.
   * **`AutoDuckProcessor`**: Remove `Math.min(pauseFrames, frames / 2)` clamping on `pauseHoldLimit`, remove the fake LFO cycle when `(maxBlockDb - minBlockDb) <= 6f`, release `target` to `0.0 dB` after `pauseFrames`, and respect `duck_thresh` directly.
   * **`TruncateSilenceProcessor`**: Compute `keep = Math.max(1, Math.round(spanLen * (compressTo.getCurrentRaw() / 100f)))` in `"Compress Excess Silence"` mode.
   * **`VocoderProcessor`**: Convert `vc_release` from milliseconds to a sample-rate-aware coefficient: `float relCoef = 1f - (float) Math.exp(-1.0 / Math.max(1.0, release.getCurrentRaw() * 0.001 * sampleRate));`.
   * **`EchoProcessor` & `MultiDelayProcessor`**: Compute `getTailFrames()` dynamically from `echo_time`/`echo_decay` and `md_time * md_echoes`; use expanding tap offsets in `Reverse Bouncing Ball`; clamp `writePos` and resize `delayLine` cleanly.
   * **`FreeverbReverbProcessor`**: Scale `COMB_TUNING`, `ALLPASS_TUNING`, and `STEREO_SPREAD` by `sampleRate / 44100.0`; clamp/reset `prePos` when `preFrames` changes or `reset()` is called.
3. **Parameter Accuracy & Pipeline Polish (P2)**:
   * Fix `FadeProcessor` `Start Gain`/`End Gain` inversion on Fade Out and pre-warm `closingLp`.
   * Fix `AudioGeneratorTool` DTMF keypad mapping (`1209/1336/1477/1633 Hz` x `697/770/852/941 Hz`), noise waveform enum labels, and selection-length handling for `Silence`.
   * Fix `AmplifyProcessor.computeEffectiveGainDb`, `ClipFixProcessor` `refPeak`, `NoiseGateExpanderProcessor` `effThresh`, `WahwahProcessor.isAudible()`, `BassAndTrebleProcessor` `link` at `0 dB`, and `LoudnessNormalizationProcessor` early return before `loud_ceiling`.
   * Scale `RawFloatPlayer.positionFrames()` by `(double) (limitFrame - startFramePos) / outFrames` during offline buffer playback so the playhead tracks time-stretched audio accurately.

FILE: FX Effects Guide.md
=================================================================================
# TakeOne FX Rack — What Each Effect Does & How to Check Every Parameter

This guide documents every effect in the Studio FX rack: what each effect does,
what every control changes, and a concrete way to verify that control with your
ears (and, where useful, with a measurement). It is written for manual testing on
a phone with headphones, but every effect also has an automated parameter matrix
(see §4) if you want numbers instead of opinions.

Notation: **Range (default)** — e.g. `20–20000 Hz (1000)` means the control
spans 20 Hz to 20 kHz and starts at 1000 Hz. `[A | B] (A)` is an enum and the
default is the first entry.

---

## 1. How the FX rack works

1. Open a take in Studio and tap **DSP FX** (the editor strip button). The rack
   replaces the Teleprompter panel.
2. Tap **+ Add Effect** and pick an effect from the searchable list. Effects are
   grouped by category: EQ & Filters, Dynamics & Mastering, Noise Removal &
   Restoration, Delay/Reverb & Spatial, Pitch/Speed & Time, Distortion/Modulation
   & Creative, Fades & Timeline Tools, Generators & Analyzers.
3. Each rack slot has:
   - a header with the effect name and `Enabled` or `Bypassed`,
   - a **Bypass/Enable** chip (the A/B switch),
   - the primary control as a dial (the one you will reach for most),
   - the remaining controls in the slot body; on curve-based effects (parametric
     EQ, graphic EQ, filter curve) they live under **Show advanced controls (N)**,
   - **Learn from selection** for the two noise-reduction effects.
4. Drag slots to reorder. Order matters: effects run top to bottom, so a
   compressor before a limiter behaves differently from a limiter before a
   compressor.
5. **Apply** bakes the enabled slots into the selected region (or the whole take
   when nothing is selected) and exits the rack. **Done** leaves the rack.
   Bypassed slots are ignored when baking.
6. Values are stored per slot and survive closing/reopening the take.

> Tip: before testing any effect, set the take's gain so peaks sit around
> −6 dBFS. Many "the effect sounds broken" reports are actually clipping or a
> too-hot input.

---

## 2. Build a test bench

You need material that contains the thing the effect acts on. The fastest way
to get repeatable material is the **Audio Generator** effect (`generator`),
which writes into the selected region:

| Signal | Generator setup | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| 1 kHz sine, −6 dBFS | Type: Tone & Chirp, Waveform: Sine/White, Start = End = 1000 Hz, 5 s | Levels, pan, distortion curves, modulation, limiter ceilings |
| 20 Hz → 20 kHz chirp | Type: Tone & Chirp, Start 20, End 20000, 10 s | EQ/filter response, notch, shelf, crossovers |
| Pink noise | Type: Noise, Waveform: Square/Pink | EQ balance, compressor behaviour, spectral effects |
| White noise | Type: Noise, Waveform: Sine/White | Noise reduction, de-hum, de-esser |
| Rhythm track | Type: Rhythm Track, Tempo 90–120 BPM | Delay timing, gate/expander, tremolo, reverse/repeat |
| Short clicks | Type: Rhythm Track (fast tempo) or hand claps | Click removal, repair, transient behaviour |
| DTMF | Type: DTMF | Spectral edit/notch checks, vocoder carriers |
| Speech | Record yourself: "Peter Piper picked…", long "sss", a plosive "P", a quiet pause | Restoration, de-esser, gate, compressor, warmth/presence, pitch/time |

Monitoring: use headphones, keep the phone volume moderate, and watch the
waveform and the peak level while you sweep a control. For stereo effects
(pan, width, phaser, tremolo phase, reverb width) listen on headphones — phone
speakers hide most of what those controls do.

---

## 3. The universal parameter check

For any control, in this order:

1. **Find neutral.** Note the default. If the effect has a bypass chip, toggle
   it: at default settings a well-behaved effect should be near-transparent
   (or intentionally subtle).
2. **Expose the dimension.** Pick a source that contains the thing the control
   governs — low frequencies for a low shelf, sibilance for a de-esser, pauses
   for a gate, a steady tone for modulation.
3. **Sweep min → max → default.** Change only that control, in sensible steps.
   Listen for the intended change first, then for side effects.
4. **Check the extremes.** Minimum/maximum are where bugs hide: silence,
   runaway gain, clicks/zipper noise, metallic artifacts, dropped tails,
   non-finite samples (the waveform collapsing or a hard digital crunch).
5. **Check interaction.** Move the effect before/after a compressor or
   limiter and confirm it still does what the label says.
6. **Save and reopen.** The value should come back and the render should match
   what you previewed.
7. **Trust the direction, not the number.** A control named "Threshold" should
   make the effect act *more* as you lower it (compressors/gates) or *less* as
   you raise it, depending on the design — the table below tells you which.

Parameter types behave differently in the UI:

- **Slider/dial** — continuous; drag slowly to hear zipper noise or stepping.
- **Enum chip** — discrete modes; each label should sound clearly different.
- **Toggle** — on/off; compare both states on the same source.
- **Action button** — runs once (e.g. *Learn from selection*); it must not
  change the audio by itself, only prepare the effect.

---

## 4. Automated checks (numbers, not ears)

The repository ships a per-effect parameter matrix. It renders every parameter
at minimum, default and maximum (every enum label, both boolean states) against
a probe that can actually show that parameter, and compares the result with the
dry reference. It also asserts physical anchors (limiter ceiling, gate closure,
hum removal, pitch/tempo ratios, reverse/invert identity).

```bash
# one effect, off-device (no emulator):
FX_EFFECT=reverb sh ./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest --tests '*FxParamMatrixDumpTest'
pip install numpy
python3 tools/fxverify/analyze.py --cases app/build/fxverify/reverb
```

In CI, each effect has its own `dsp-matrix (<effect-id>)` shard inside the
**FX Parameter Verification** workflow, and `tools/fxverify/check_drift.py`
fails the run if an effect exists in code but not in the matrix. The flag file
`app/build/fxverify/<id>/verdicts.json` lists, per parameter, whether it moved
the audio, by how much, and whether that movement matched the expected
direction.

Use this guide's tables to interpret those verdicts: the "What it does" column
is the expected direction, and the "How to check" column is what a human should
hear when the matrix says the parameter moved.

---

## 5. Effect reference

The sections below follow the rack categories. Every registered effect is
covered, including the role-scoped Warmth and Presence entries.

### EQ & FILTERS

---

#### 1. Low-Cut Filter Pro (`hpf`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

A clean Butterworth high-pass for removing rumble, handling noise, wind and
plosive thumps. It is the "set and forget" first stage of a vocal chain; the
24 dB/oct mode cascades two second-order sections so the cutoff is steeper
without a resonant peak. Coefficients glide so scrubbing the cutoff does not
click.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cutoff | `40–160 Hz (80)` | Frequency below which content is attenuated. | Speak with "P"/"B" plosives and raise the cutoff toward 160 Hz: thumps and desk rumble disappear while the voice stays. At 40 Hz almost nothing changes. |
| Slope | `[12 dB/oct \| 24 dB/oct] (24)` | Steepness of the filter below the cutoff. | A/B the two slopes on the same rumble: 24 dB/oct removes noticeably more sub-bass. Check that 24 dB/oct does not add a boom at the corner (it should stay smooth). |

**Quick test:** record "Peter Piper picked a peck" close to the mic; cutoff 80,
slope 24 should remove the plosive thump without thinning the voice.

---

#### 2. High-Pass Filter (`highpass`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

A sweepable high-pass with six roll-off strengths (6–48 dB/oct). Where the
Low-Cut Pro is a vocal-chain tool with a narrow range, this is the general-purpose
high-pass: use it to remove everything below the useful band, or to isolate
highs for a check.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cutoff | `20–20000 Hz (80)` | Corner below which content is attenuated. | Feed the 20 Hz → 20 kHz chirp and raise the cutoff: the sweep should vanish below the displayed frequency and pass above it. At 20 Hz it is effectively off. |
| Roll-Off | `[6 \| 12 \| 18 \| 24 \| 36 \| 48 dB/oct] (12)` | Filter steepness. | Compare 6 vs 48 dB/oct on the chirp: steeper slopes cut more just below the corner. Check high orders for ringing on a click/plosive. |

**Quick test:** chirp sweep with cutoff 1 kHz: only the upper part of the sweep
should remain; every step up the roll-off list should make the transition
sharper.

---

#### 3. Low-Pass Filter (`lowpass`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

The mirror of the high-pass: removes hiss, harshness and high-frequency noise
above the cutoff. Same six roll-off strengths.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cutoff | `20–20000 Hz (12000)` | Corner above which content is attenuated. | With the chirp, lower the cutoff: the top of the sweep disappears. At 12 kHz you hear a duller, darker version of speech; at 2 kHz it sounds like a telephone. |
| Roll-Off | `[6 \| 12 \| 18 \| 24 \| 36 \| 48 dB/oct] (12)` | Filter steepness. | Compare 6 vs 48 dB/oct: 6 leaves audible "air" just above the corner; 48 removes it abruptly. Listen for a metallic ring at extreme slopes. |

**Quick test:** hiss recording → cutoff 6–8 kHz, roll-off 24: hiss drops, speech
stays intelligible; then push cutoff to 2 kHz and confirm the expected
telephone-band sound.

---

#### 4. Notch Filter (`notch`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

A surgical notch for removing a single frequency: mains hum (50/60 Hz) or a
ringing resonance. It is a very narrow RBJ notch — the point is to remove the
tone while leaving the voice around it untouched.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Quick Pick | `[Custom \| 50 Hz hum \| 60 Hz hum] (Custom)` | Presets that jump the frequency to a mains hum. | Record/import hum and switch between presets: each should null its named hum. `Custom` leaves your frequency alone. |
| Frequency | `20–20000 Hz (60)` | Center of the notch. | Sweep slowly around 50/60 Hz on a hum recording until the hum disappears. On the chirp, the sweep should have a narrow hole at this frequency. |
| Q | `0.1–30.0 (5.0)` | Notch width: high Q = narrow (surgical), low Q = wide (removes more around the center). | At Q 30 only the exact tone goes; at Q 0.5 a broad band disappears. Use high Q on a steady hum so the voice is untouched, and confirm no audible hole in speech. |

**Quick test:** 60 Hz hum take → Quick Pick "60 Hz hum" → hum vanishes, voice
unchanged; then lower Q to 1 and hear the voice get thinner (proof the width
control works).

---

#### 5. Shelf Filter (`shelf`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

A broad low or high shelf with an adjustable slope. Use it for overall tonal
balance: more body (low shelf) or more air/brightness (high shelf).

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shelf Type | `[Low Shelf \| High Shelf] (Low Shelf)` | Which end of the spectrum is shaped. | Low shelf 200 Hz +12 dB adds body to speech; high shelf 3 kHz +12 dB adds brightness. Switching type should move the effect to the other end. |
| Corner Freq | `20–20000 Hz (200)` | Where the shelf starts to act. | With pink noise, a low shelf at 80 Hz boosts only the bottom; at 1 kHz it boosts a large part of the voice. Hear the corner move. |
| Shelf Gain | `-24.0–24.0 dB (0.0)` | Amount of boost/cut. | ±24 dB should be obvious and symmetric; 0 dB must be transparent. Check that large boosts do not clip the output (watch peaks). |
| Slope S | `0.3–2.0 (0.7)` | Shape of the transition into the shelf: lower = gentler, higher = steeper. | On pink noise, compare 0.3 and 2.0: the shelf edge becomes more abrupt; check that 2.0 does not ring. |

**Quick test:** pink noise + high shelf at 4 kHz: raise gain from 0 to +18 dB and
back; sweep the corner from 1 to 12 kHz to hear the transition point move.

---

#### 6. 6-Band Parametric EQ (`eq6`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

A console-style EQ: low cut, four musical bands (band 2 can be a low shelf or
bell, band 5 a high shelf or bell), and a high cut. The slot shows a curve
canvas you can drag; numeric controls live under **Show advanced controls**.
The primary value on the rack is the EQ output trim.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low-Cut Freq | `20–1000 Hz (80)` | High-pass corner at the bottom of the EQ. | At 20 Hz it is effectively off; raise to 120–200 Hz and hear rumble/thump disappear. Confirm the voice does not get thin at 80 Hz. |
| Low-Cut Slope | `[12 dB/oct \| 24 dB/oct] (12)` | Steepness of the low cut. | Compare on a plosive: 24 dB/oct removes more sub-bass; check for a resonant boom at the corner. |
| Band 2 Type | `[Low Shelf \| Bell] (Low Shelf)` | Shape of band 2. | Shelf: broad low-end tilt; Bell: a focused boost/cut. Switch types and confirm the character changes (shelf affects everything below the frequency, bell only around it). |
| Band 2 Freq | `40–500 Hz (120)` | Corner/center of band 2. | On pink noise, sweep 40→500 Hz: the boosted region moves from sub-bass to chest voice. |
| Band 2 Gain | `-18.0–18.0 dB (0.0)` | Boost/cut of band 2. | +12 dB adds chest/body, −12 dB removes boom. 0 dB must be flat. |
| Band 2 Q | `0.3–10.0 (0.7)` | Band 2 width (bell) / shelf transition (shelf). | In Bell mode, Q 10 is a narrow peak; Q 0.3 is broad. In shelf mode it sets how quickly the shelf transitions. |
| Band 3 Freq | `150–2500 Hz (500)` | Center of the low-mid bell. | Sweep while boosting +12 dB: 150 Hz = mud, 500 Hz = boxiness, 2 kHz = honk. |
| Band 3 Gain | `-18.0–18.0 dB (0.0)` | Boost/cut of band 3. | The classic "mud cut" is 300–500 Hz at −3…−6 dB; confirm it clears the voice. |
| Band 3 Q | `0.3–10.0 (1.0)` | Width of band 3. | Narrow Q cuts only the boxy tone; wide Q changes the whole low-mid balance. |
| Band 4 Freq | `600–8000 Hz (2500)` | Center of the presence bell. | Boost +9 dB around 2.5–3 kHz to hear consonants jump forward; 6 kHz is sibilance. |
| Band 4 Gain | `-18.0–18.0 dB (0.0)` | Boost/cut of band 4. | +9 dB should make speech cut through; −9 dB should soften it. Watch for harshness. |
| Band 4 Q | `0.3–10.0 (1.0)` | Width of band 4. | High Q = surgical de-ess-like notch; low Q = broad presence tilt. |
| Band 5 Type | `[High Shelf \| Bell] (High Shelf)` | Shape of band 5. | Shelf = air/brightness; Bell = focused peak. Switch and hear the difference on a "sss". |
| Band 5 Freq | `2000–18000 Hz (8000)` | Corner/center of band 5. | On pink noise, sweep 2→18 kHz: the boost moves from presence to air. |
| Band 5 Gain | `-18.0–18.0 dB (0.0)` | Boost/cut of band 5. | +6 dB adds air; −6 dB tames hiss. Check that +18 dB does not become painful (it should still be controlled). |
| Band 5 Q | `0.3–10.0 (0.7)` | Width (bell) / transition (shelf) of band 5. | Compare narrow vs wide on a cymbal/noise source. |
| High-Cut Freq | `2000–20000 Hz (20000)` | Low-pass corner at the top. | At 20 kHz it is effectively off; lower to 8–10 kHz and hear the top end go. |
| High-Cut Slope | `[12 dB/oct \| 24 dB/oct] (12)` | Steepness of the high cut. | 24 dB/oct removes more air; check for a "swishy" transition. |
| Output Gain | `-18.0–18.0 dB (0.0)` | Final trim for the EQ. | Boost a band and use output to compensate: the voice should get louder without changing tone. 0 dB must be unity. |

**Quick test:** chirp + pink noise; drag each band on the curve while it plays.
Every band should create a local bump/dip at its frequency, Q should change the
bump's width, and switching band 2/5 between shelf and bell should change a
local peak into a broad tilt.

---

#### 7. Graphic EQ (`geq`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

A constant-Q graphic EQ: 10 ISO octave bands (31.5 Hz–16 kHz) or 31 one-third-octave
bands (20 Hz–20 kHz), ±18 dB each, plus output trim. Use it for quick broad
shaping or for removing a specific octave.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Layout | `[10 bands (ISO) \| 31 bands (1/3 oct)] (10 bands)` | Switches between octave and third-octave band sets. | Switch layouts on pink noise: 10 bands = broad strokes; 31 bands = surgical. The band controls should change to match. |
| Output Gain | `-18.0–18.0 dB (0.0)` | Final trim. | Boost one band +12 dB and pull output down: tone changes, level returns. 0 dB must be unity. |
| Band 1…N | `-18.0–18.0 dB (0.0)` each | Boost/cut for that band. | On pink noise, boost 1 kHz +12 dB: only that octave (or third) jumps. Cut 250 Hz: boxiness drops. Check that adjacent bands overlap smoothly and that 0 dB is flat. |

**Quick test:** pink noise → boost 500 Hz and 2 kHz alternately; each should
produce a clearly different "honk" and "presence" colour without affecting the
rest of the spectrum.

---

#### 8. Filter Curve EQ (`fcurve`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

A draw-your-own linear-phase EQ: up to 32 frequency/gain nodes define the
magnitude curve, and the audio runs through a 1024/2048/4096-tap FIR convolution.
Use it when you want a precise, phase-linear response (classical mastering-style
curves, matching a reference) rather than the character of an IIR EQ.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Output | `-18.0–18.0 dB (0.0)` | Final trim after the FIR. | With a neutral curve, changing output should only change level, not tone. |
| Points | `2–32 (8)` | Number of active nodes. | Raise from 2 to 32: you get more nodes to shape with. Dropping the count must remove the extra nodes without glitches. |
| Precision | `[1024 \| 2048 \| 4096 taps] (2048)` | FIR length: more taps = sharper low-frequency resolution, more latency. | A narrow 40 Hz cut is soft at 1024 and clean at 4096. Confirm the latency changes (the preview/commit alignment handles it) and that the tone matches at all three. |
| F1…Fn | `20–20000 Hz` (defaults span 40 Hz–16 kHz) | Node frequencies (draggable on the curve). | Move one node across the spectrum while boosting it: the bump should follow the node exactly. |
| G1…Gn | `-24.0–24.0 dB (0.0)` | Node gains. | Set one node to +12 and another to −12: you should hear a broad shape, not a narrow spike. Check that a flat curve (all gains 0) is transparent. |

**Quick test:** draw a gentle "smile" (low +4 dB, mid −3 dB, high +3 dB) on pink
noise; compare 1024 vs 4096 taps — the shape should stay the same while the
low-frequency precision improves.

---

#### 9. Bass & Treble (`basstreble`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

The classic two-knob tone stack: a 250 Hz low shelf and a 3.5 kHz high shelf,
plus output volume and a link switch. It is the fastest way to tilt a take.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bass (250 Hz) | `-30.0–30.0 dB (0.0)` | Low-shelf boost/cut. | +12 dB adds weight, −12 dB thins the bottom. On speech, 250 Hz is chest/body; confirm it does not become muddy at +30. |
| Treble (3.5 kHz) | `-30.0–30.0 dB (0.0)` | High-shelf boost/cut. | +12 dB adds articulation/air, −12 dB makes it dull. Check that +30 dB does not turn into harsh hiss. |
| Volume | `-18.0–18.0 dB (0.0)` | Output trim. | Compensate a big bass/treble boost and confirm the level returns without tone change. 0 dB = unity. |
| Link Bass & Treble | `off/on (off)` | Ties the two shelves together (adjusting one moves the other by the same amount). | Turn it on and move Bass: Treble should follow. Turn it off and confirm they move independently. |

**Quick test:** speech → Bass +9, Treble +6, Volume −4: fuller and brighter at
roughly the same loudness; then link the controls and confirm they track.

---

#### 10. Classic Filters (`classic`)

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

Analog-prototype IIR filters: Butterworth (maximally flat passband), Chebyshev I
(equiripple passband), Chebyshev II (equiripple stopband) and Bessel (flat group
delay), orders 1–10, low-pass or high-pass. This is the "textbook filter" effect
for checking filter behaviour or creating extreme band-limiting.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prototype | `[Butterworth \| Chebyshev I \| Chebyshev II \| Bessel] (Butterworth)` | Filter family. | On a chirp: Butterworth is smooth, Chebyshev I ripples in the passband, Chebyshev II ripples just before the stopband, Bessel keeps transients cleanest. Each must sound different. |
| Passband | `[Low-Pass \| High-Pass] (Low-Pass)` | Direction of the filter. | Flip it: the same cutoff should swap from keeping lows to keeping highs. |
| Order | `1–10 (4)` | Filter steepness (number of poles). | Order 1 is very gentle; order 10 is almost a brick wall. On a chirp, each step should make the transition sharper. Check high orders for ringing on clicks. |
| Cutoff | `20–20000 Hz (1000)` | Corner frequency. | Sweep it on the chirp: the transition follows the displayed frequency. |
| Ripple | `0.1–6.0 dB (1.0)` | Passband (Chebyshev I) or stopband (Chebyshev II) ripple; ignored by Butterworth/Bessel. | In Chebyshev I, raise ripple and listen for a wavy passband on pink noise; in Chebyshev II the ripple appears near the stopband. Butterworth/Bessel should not change. |

**Quick test:** chirp → Butterworth LP 1 kHz order 4 is smooth; switch to
Chebyshev I and raise ripple to 6 dB to hear the passband ripple; switch to
Bessel and confirm the transient (click) stays cleaner.

---

#### 11. Warmth & Vocal Presence (`tone`) — also `warmth` and `presence`

*Category: EQ & Filters.*

Two musical shelves in one processor: a low shelf around 180 Hz for chest/body
("warmth") and a high shelf around 3.5 kHz for articulation and air
("presence"). The rack can host them as one combined effect
(`Warmth & Vocal Presence`), or as role-scoped effects that expose only their
own two controls (`Warmth & Chest Body`, `Vocal Presence & Air`). When both
slots are separated by another effect in the rack, the engine splits the tone
stage around that effect so the order is honoured.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Warmth | `0–100% (tone 40, warmth 40, presence n/a)` | Amount of low-shelf boost around the warmth corner. | On a male voice, 30–50% adds body; 100% should be obviously full/boomy. At 0% the low shelf must be transparent. |
| Warmth Corner | `80–350 Hz (180)` | Where the low shelf starts. | Lower (80–120 Hz) = sub/chest weight; higher (250–350 Hz) = boxy low-mid. Sweep it on speech and hear the weight move. |
| Presence | `0–100% (tone 45, presence 45, warmth n/a)` | Amount of high-shelf boost around the presence corner. | 30–60% makes consonants clearer; 100% can be harsh. At 0% it must be transparent. |
| Presence Corner | `1500–6500 Hz (3500)` | Where the high shelf starts. | 1.5–2.5 kHz = forward/nasal; 4–6.5 kHz = air/sibilance. Sweep it on a "sss" and confirm the brightness moves. |

**Quick test:** speech → Warmth 50%, corner 150 Hz (fuller); Presence 40%, corner
4 kHz (clearer). Then add a Compressor between them in the rack and confirm the
warmth/presence order still matches the slot order (this is the split-tone
path).

### DYNAMICS & MASTERING

---

#### 12. Amplify (`amplify`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

Two-pass gain: the processor scans the selection's peak, applies the requested
gain, and (unless you allow clipping) limits the result so the peak does not
exceed the **New Peak Amplitude** target. With **Amplification** at 0 it acts as
a peak normalizer; with a non-zero value it is a plain gain stage that is still
capped to the target unless clipping is allowed.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amplification | `-50.0–50.0 dB (0.0)` | Fixed gain applied to the selection. | Quiet take: +12 dB should be obviously louder. 0 dB must be unity. At −50 dB the take should almost disappear. |
| New Peak Amplitude | `-40.0–0.0 dB (0.0)` | Target peak. With Amplification at 0 this normalizes the take to this peak. | Set Amplification 0 and New Peak −6 dB on a quiet take: the waveform peak should land at −6. Set −1: louder, still below full scale. |
| Allow Clipping | `off/on (off)` | When off, samples are clamped below 0 dBFS; when on, gain is not capped by the target and can clip. | Hot take + positive gain: with clipping off the peaks flatten safely at the ceiling; turn it on and hear/see the hard clip. |

**Quick test:** quiet speech → Amplification 0, New Peak −6 (normalized); then
Amplification +12 with clipping off (peak capped) vs on (audible crunch).

---

#### 13. Normalize (`normalize`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

DC-offset removal plus peak or RMS normalization, with linked or independent
stereo. Peak normalization makes the loudest sample hit the target; RMS
normalization raises the average level instead, which usually sounds louder but
leaves less headroom.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Remove DC Offset | `off/on (on)` | Centers the waveform by subtracting its average. | A take with visible vertical offset (waveform not centered) should re-center. On a clean take it must be inaudible. |
| Normalize Peak Amplitude | `off/on (on)` | Enables peak normalization. | Off = no peak normalization (only DC/RMS behaviour). On = the peak moves to the target. |
| Target Peak | `-60.0–0.0 dB (-1.0)` | Peak (or RMS) level to normalize to. | −1 dB is loud and safe; −6 dB leaves headroom; −40 dB is nearly silent. Check the waveform peak matches the label. |
| Normalize Stereo Channels Independently | `off/on (off)` | Off = one gain for both channels (keeps balance); on = each channel normalized on its own. | Take with a quiet left and loud right: off keeps the imbalance, on brings both channels to the same level. |
| Normalize to RMS instead of Peak | `off/on (off)` | Switches the target from peak to RMS. | On speech, RMS mode is louder for the same target and the peaks sit lower; check for clipping on transient-heavy material. |

**Quick test:** unbalanced stereo take → target −3 dB; toggle independent
normalization and watch one channel jump while the other stays.

---

#### 14. Loudness Normalization (`loudness`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

EBU R128 / ITU-R BS.1770-4 loudness normalization with a true-peak ceiling:
it measures integrated LUFS over gated 400 ms blocks and applies one gain so
the program lands on the target, then clamps true peaks to the ceiling. Use it
to match takes to a platform target (−16 LUFS is a common streaming level,
−23 LUFS is broadcast).

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Target Loudness | `-70.0–0.0 dB (-16.0)` | Integrated loudness target in LUFS. | Normalize a quiet take to −16: it should be clearly louder; −23 should be ~7 dB quieter than −16. Use an external LUFS meter to confirm. |
| True-Peak Ceiling | `-9.0–-0.1 dB (-1.0)` | Maximum true peak after normalization. | With a transient-heavy take, normalizing loud should pin peaks at the ceiling instead of clipping. Lower the ceiling to −3 and hear the level come down. |
| Dual Mono | `off/on (off)` | Measures/normalizes the channels as two independent mono signals. | On a dual-mono take, enabling it should match both channels; on real stereo it changes the measurement (and therefore the gain). |

**Quick test:** quiet speech → target −16, ceiling −1: loud and clean; then
target −23 and confirm the take is roughly 7 LU quieter.

---

#### 15. Compressor (`dyncomp`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

A full-featured compressor with a noise-floor freeze (so silence is not pumped
up), soft knee, Peak/RMS detection, and a downward/upward mode. Downward
compression reduces loud parts; upward compression raises quiet parts. The
noise-floor control freezes gain reduction below a level so room tone does not
breathe.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Threshold | `-60.0–-1.0 dB (-18.0)` | Level where compression starts. Lower = more compression. | Speech with peaks around −12 dB: at −18 only the loudest syllables compress; at −40 the whole take is squashed. |
| Noise Floor | `-80.0–-20.0 dB (-55.0)` | Below this level the detector freezes, preventing silence from being boosted. | Record speech with a quiet pause: with the floor high, the pause stays quiet; with it low, the noise pumps up between words. |
| Ratio | `1.1–20.0:1 (3.0)` | How strongly levels above the threshold are reduced. | 1.1:1 is nearly transparent; 10:1 flattens dynamics. Confirm the compressor acts *more* as the ratio rises. |
| Attack | `1.0–200.0 ms (10.0)` | How fast gain reduction engages. | Fast attack (1–5 ms) tames plosives but can dull transients; slow (50–200 ms) lets transients through. Compare on a click/plosive. |
| Release | `10.0–2000.0 ms (150.0)` | How fast gain returns after the signal drops. | Short release pumps/ducks; long release smooths and sustains. Hear the difference on speech with pauses. |
| Knee Width | `0.0–20.0 dB (6.0)` | Softness of the threshold transition. | 0 dB = hard knee (audible "grab"), 20 dB = gradual. On a slowly rising tone the onset of compression should soften. |
| Detector | `[Peak \| RMS] (RMS)` | Peak follows sample peaks; RMS follows average energy. | Peak clamps transients hard; RMS breathes with the overall level. On a drum-like signal the difference is obvious. |
| Upward Compression | `off/on (off)` | Inverts the action: raises quiet parts toward the threshold instead of lowering loud parts. | Off = normal downward compression. On = the quiet parts come up; check that the noise floor is not exaggerated. |
| Make-Up Gain | `-12.0–24.0 dB (0.0)` | Output gain after compression. | Compress heavily and raise make-up to restore loudness; it should not change the compressed dynamics. |

**Quick test:** speech with a noisy pause → threshold −24, ratio 4:1, fast
attack, 150 ms release: words even out; raise Noise Floor until the pause stops
breathing; switch to Upward and hear the quiet syllables lift.

---

#### 16. Compressor Pro (`comp`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

A simple vocal leveler: one **Compression** amount drives a soft-knee
compressor with automatic, gated make-up. Because the make-up is gated, room
tone before speech is not amplified.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compression | `0–100% (0)` | Overall amount of compression (and automatic make-up). | 0% must be transparent. 40–60% evens out speech; 100% is heavily controlled. Confirm the take gets denser, not just quieter. |
| Ratio | `1.2–10.0:1 (3.0)` | Slope above the internal threshold. | With Compression at 50%, raising the ratio should flatten peaks further. |
| Attack | `1.0–100.0 ms (8.0)` | Engagement speed. | Fast attack softens plosives; slow attack keeps consonant transients crisp. |
| Release | `10.0–1000.0 ms (140.0)` | Recovery speed. | Short release sounds lively but can pump; long release is smoother. Check on speech with pauses. |
| Knee | `0.0–18.0 dB (6.0)` | Softness of the onset. | 0 dB grabs abruptly; 18 dB eases in. Listen on a sustained vowel. |

**Quick test:** alternating loud/quiet speech → Compression 50% should even it
out; confirm the silent gap before the first word stays quiet (gated make-up).

#### 17. Multiband Compressor (`mbcomp`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

Splits the signal into three bands (low/mid/high) at two crossovers and
compresses each independently, then sums them. Use it to control a boomy low
end without dulling the highs, or to tame harsh upper-mids without touching the
bass.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low Crossover | `80.0–500.0 Hz (200.0)` | Boundary between the low and mid bands. | On pink noise with the low band compressing, moving the crossover shifts which frequencies pump. |
| High Crossover | `1500.0–8000.0 Hz (3200.0)` | Boundary between the mid and high bands. | Move it while compressing the high band: the "sss" region starts being controlled at a different point. |
| Low Threshold | `-48.0–-3.0 dB (-20.0)` | Compression threshold for the low band. | Lower it: bass/boom gets controlled. Confirm the mids stay untouched. |
| Low Ratio | `1.2–10.0:1 (3.0)` | Low-band compression amount. | Raise it and hear the low end flatten on a bass-heavy take. |
| Mid Threshold | `-48.0–-3.0 dB (-18.0)` | Compression threshold for the mid band. | Lower it to tame boxy/honky mids; confirm lows/highs are unaffected. |
| Mid Ratio | `1.2–10.0:1 (2.5)` | Mid-band compression amount. | Compare 2.5 vs 10 on speech: the mid band becomes progressively flatter. |
| High Threshold | `-48.0–-3.0 dB (-22.0)` | Compression threshold for the high band. | Lower it to control harshness/sibilance; check that it does not dull the air too much. |
| High Ratio | `1.2–10.0:1 (3.5)` | High-band compression amount. | Raise it on a bright take: the top end smooths. |
| Overall Amount | `0–100% (65)` | Blends all three compressed bands with the dry signal. | 0% should be transparent; 100% is full multiband control. Sweep it to hear the whole compression appear. |

**Quick test:** bass-heavy speech → low threshold −30, low ratio 6:1, overall
70%: boom is controlled while the voice stays open; then move the low crossover
and hear the control point shift.

---

#### 18. Brickwall Limiter (`bricklim`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

A 3 ms look-ahead brickwall limiter with a soft-clip knee and optional auto
make-up. It is the safety stage: drive into it and the output peak should never
exceed the ceiling.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Input Gain | `0.0–24.0 dB (0.0)` | Gain before limiting (how hard you drive it). | Raise it on a mix: the limiter works harder, the take gets louder, and the peak stays at the ceiling. |
| Ceiling | `-15.0–-0.05 dB (-0.3)` | Maximum output peak. | Watch the waveform peak: it should sit at the ceiling, never above. Lower the ceiling to −6 and hear the level drop. |
| Release | `5.0–500.0 ms (60.0)` | Recovery after limiting. | Fast release is punchy but can distort low frequencies; slow release is smoother. Check on bass-heavy material. |
| Soft-Clip Knee | `off/on (on)` | Rounds peaks approaching the ceiling instead of hard-limiting. | On = less brittle on transients; off = harder, more obvious limiting. Compare on a clap/plosive. |
| Auto Make-Up | `off/on (off)` | Restores loudness lost to limiting. | Drive hard with it off, then on: the output should come back up while still respecting the ceiling. |

**Quick test:** hot take → Input Gain +12, ceiling −1: peaks pinned at −1 dBFS;
sweep the ceiling from −0.3 to −6 and watch the waveform top follow it.

---

#### 19. Brickwall Limiter Pro (`limiter`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

The always-on ceiling limiter. At **Drive 0** it is a safety ceiling only:
signals below the ceiling pass untouched and only peaks approaching it are
shaped. Raising Drive pushes the signal into the ceiling for loudness.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Drive | `0–100% (0)` | Amount of gain pushed into the soft-clip ceiling (up to the limiter's maximum drive). | 0% must be transparent for signals below the ceiling. 50–100% should get louder while peaks stop at the ceiling. |
| Ceiling | `-6.0–-0.1 dBFS (-0.2)` | Maximum output level. | Watch peaks: they should never cross the value. Lowering the ceiling should lower the output level, not create clipping. |
| Release | `10.0–500.0 ms (80.0)` | Recovery time of the limiter. | Short release can pump/distort bass; long release is smoother. Compare on a bass note. |

**Quick test:** a signal that peaks at −1 dBFS with Drive 0 should pass nearly
unchanged; Drive 100% should be louder with the waveform top flat at the
ceiling.

---

#### 20. Gate / Expander (`gateexp`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

A noise gate / downward expander with hysteresis, hold, ratio, range and a
sidechain high-pass. In **Expander** mode quiet signals are faded down by the
ratio; in **Gate** mode they are cut to the range floor. The sidechain HPF stops
rumble from holding the gate open.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mode | `[Gate \| Expander] (Expander)` | Gate = hard close; Expander = gradual downward expansion. | On room tone, Gate snaps shut; Expander fades it. Both should reduce noise between phrases. |
| Threshold | `-96.0–-6.0 dB (-42.0)` | Level where the gate opens/closes. | Raise it until room noise closes but speech still opens it. Confirm the voice does not get chopped. |
| Hysteresis | `0.0–12.0 dB (4.0)` | Gap between open and close thresholds; prevents chatter. | At 0 dB a signal near the threshold stutters; raising it makes the open/close stable. |
| Ratio | `1.5–20.0:1 (4.0)` | Expander slope below the threshold. | In Expander mode, higher ratios attenuate quiet parts more strongly. |
| Range / Floor | `-90.0–0.0 dB (-24.0)` | Maximum attenuation when closed. | At −24 dB the noise is reduced but audible; at −90 it is silent. Check the floor on a quiet pause. |
| Attack | `1.0–100.0 ms (3.0)` | How fast the gate opens. | Fast attack catches word onsets; slow attack can clip the first consonant. |
| Hold | `0.0–1000.0 ms (40.0)` | Keeps the gate open after the signal drops. | Increase it so short gaps between words do not close the gate (no chopping). |
| Release | `10.0–2000.0 ms (180.0)` | How fast it closes/fades down. | Short release sounds abrupt/tail-cutting; long release sounds natural but lets noise linger. |
| Sidechain HPF | `20.0–600.0 Hz (120.0)` | High-pass on the detector signal. | With desk rumble, a higher HPF stops the rumble from opening the gate; the voice still opens it. |

**Quick test:** speech + room tone → threshold until the pauses close, hold
~100 ms so word gaps do not chop, release ~200 ms; then tap the desk and confirm
the sidechain HPF stops the thump from opening the gate.

---

#### 21. Auto Duck (`autoduck`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

Ducks the signal whenever the input exceeds the threshold — the classic
"music bed under a voice" tool. It ramps down quickly, holds through short
pauses, and ramps back up smoothly.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Duck Amount | `-36.0–0.0 dB (-12.0)` | How far the signal is reduced while ducking. | On a music bed, −12 dB is a gentle dip; −36 dB is nearly muted. 0 dB should not duck at all. |
| Threshold | `-60.0–-3.0 dB (-28.0)` | Input level that triggers ducking. | Speak over the bed: lower the threshold until the voice reliably triggers the duck; too low and room tone triggers it. |
| Fade Down | `10–2000 ms (120)` | Ramp-down time. | Short = instant duck (can click); long = the first word may be masked. Check the start of a phrase. |
| Fade Up | `10–3000 ms (400)` | Ramp-up time after the trigger stops. | Long = smooth recovery; short = the bed jumps back. Listen after a phrase. |
| Max Pause | `50–5000 ms (500)` | Hold time across brief pauses before releasing. | Speak with pauses shorter than this value: the bed should stay ducked instead of pumping between words. |

**Quick test:** voice over a music/room bed → threshold set so speech triggers,
amount −15 dB, fade down 100 ms, fade up 500 ms, max pause 600 ms: the bed dips
under speech and stays down through short pauses.

---

#### 22. De-Esser (Split Band) (`deesssplit`)

*Category: Dynamics & Mastering.*

A precision sibilance compressor: a band around the **Frequency** is detected
and reduced, either split-band (only the sibilant band is attenuated) or
broadband (the whole signal is ducked). The threshold and max reduction make the
behaviour predictable.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Frequency | `3000–12000 Hz (6800)` | Center of the sibilance band. | On a long "sss", sweep the frequency: the reduction should be strongest when it matches the hiss. 6–8 kHz is typical for "s". |
| Bandwidth Q | `0.5–10.0 (2.0)` | Width of the detector band. | High Q = only the exact sibilant; low Q = a wider band. Compare on "sh" vs "s". |
| Threshold | `-48.0–0.0 dB (-18.0)` | Level where reduction starts. | Lower it: more sibilance is caught. Too low and normal consonants get dulled. |
| Max Reduction | `0.0–24.0 dB (12.0)` | Ceiling on how much the band can be reduced. | 3–6 dB is gentle; 24 dB is heavy. Confirm "sss" is tamed without a lisp. |
| Mode | `[Split-Band \| Broadband] (Split-Band)` | Split-band attenuates only the band; broadband ducks the whole signal. | Split-band keeps the vowel untouched; broadband dips the whole word on an "s". Compare on "seventy-six". |

**Quick test:** read "She sells seashells" → Frequency 6.8 kHz, threshold −24,
max 8 dB, split-band: hiss softens, vowels unchanged; switch to broadband and
hear the whole word dip.

### NOISE REMOVAL & RESTORATION

---

#### 23. Noise Suppression Pro (`noise`)

*Category: Noise Removal & Restoration.*

Spectral noise subtraction with a learned noise profile. Select a noise-only
region, tap **Learn from selection** in the slot, then apply the effect to the
take: the learned spectrum is subtracted from every frame while loud voice bins
are left alone. With no learned profile it falls back to an adaptive minimum
tracker, so it still does something out of the box (less precisely).

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intensity | `0–100% (50)` | How much of the learned noise spectrum is subtracted. | On a hissy take, 20–40% is gentle, 80–100% is aggressive. Too high produces "underwater"/metallic artifacts; confirm the voice stays natural. |
| Smoothing | `0–100% (50)` | Smooths the subtraction over frequency/time, trading detail for fewer artifacts. | Low smoothing keeps more detail but can sound "chirpy"; high smoothing reduces musical noise but can dull consonants. Compare on an "sss". |
| Learn from selection | action button | Captures the noise profile from the current selection. | Select 1–2 s of noise only (no voice), tap Learn, then apply: hiss should drop. Re-learn from a noisy region and confirm the result changes. |

**Quick test:** record 3 s of room tone, then speech. Select the room tone, tap
**Learn from selection**, apply to the speech: hiss drops, voice intact; push
Intensity to 100% and hear the artifacts (proof the control works).

---

#### 24. Spectral Noise Reduction (`specnr`)

*Category: Noise Removal & Restoration.*

A second spectral denoiser with explicit dB controls. It learns a per-bin noise
profile from a selection and applies spectral gating; **Sensitivity** controls
over-subtraction and **Freq Smoothing** controls how many neighboring bins are
smoothed. **Reduce Noise** outputs the cleaned signal; **Isolate Noise** outputs
what is being removed (useful to hear exactly what the effect is doing).

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Noise Reduction | `0.0–48.0 dB (18.0)` | Maximum attenuation applied to bins judged noise. | At 6 dB the noise is softened; at 48 dB it is nearly removed but artifacts increase. |
| Sensitivity | `0.0–24.0 dB (6.0)` | Over-subtraction: higher values treat more bins as noise. | Raise it and hear more noise disappear — and more voice detail go with it. |
| Freq Smoothing | `0–12 bins (2)` | Smooths the gain curve across neighboring bins. | 0 bins can sound granular; 12 bins is smoother but smears narrow tones. Check on a steady hiss and on speech. |
| Mode | `[Reduce Noise \| Isolate Noise] (Reduce Noise)` | Reduce = cleaned output; Isolate = the removed component only. | Switch to Isolate: you should hear hiss/room tone and almost no voice. This is the clearest proof the learned profile is correct. |
| Learn from selection | action button | Captures the per-bin noise profile. | Select noise only, Learn, then switch between Reduce/Isolate: Isolate should sound like the selected noise. |

**Quick test:** hum + hiss take → learn from a noise-only region → Reduce with
18 dB / 6 dB sensitivity: noise drops; Isolate should contain the removed noise
only.

---

#### 25. Click Removal (`declick`)

*Category: Noise Removal & Restoration.*

Detects short impulsive clicks, pops and mouth ticks by their second-order
curvature relative to the surrounding neighborhood and replaces them with cubic
Hermite interpolation, leaving the rest of the audio untouched.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Threshold | `1–900 (200)` | Detection sensitivity: lower values catch smaller clicks, higher values only strong ones. | On a take with a clear click, lower the threshold until it disappears. Too low and the effect starts dulling normal transients. |
| Max Spike Width | `1–40 samples (12)` | Longest click the interpolator may replace. | A wide pop needs a bigger width; setting it too small leaves part of the click. Check a short tick vs a longer pop. |

**Quick test:** add a click (tap the mic or use a rhythm track), set width 12:
lower the threshold until the click vanishes; confirm speech transients survive
at that setting.

---

#### 26. Clip Fix (`clipfix`)

*Category: Noise Removal & Restoration.*

Repairs flat-topped clipped waveforms: it finds runs that sit at the clipping
threshold, reduces the whole take by the requested headroom to make room, and
reconstructs each run with a cubic arch matching the entry/exit slopes.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Clipping Threshold | `80–100% (95)` | How close to the peak a sample must be to count as clipped. | Set it just below the recorded clipping level (e.g. 95%). Too low treats loud peaks as clipped; too high leaves flat tops. |
| Restore Headroom | `-18.0–0.0 dB (-6.0)` | Gain reduction applied before rebuilding peaks. | More headroom gives the arch room but lowers the take; less keeps level but limits the repair. Check the waveform top becomes rounded instead of flat. |

**Quick test:** a deliberately clipped recording (record too hot) → threshold 95%,
headroom −6 dB: flat tops become rounded; confirm the take is slightly quieter
and less crunchy.

---

#### 27. Repair (`repair`)

*Category: Noise Removal & Restoration.*

LPC interpolation for a short glitch or dropout: it finds the worst span in the
region and reconstructs it from the audio on both sides using forward and
backward linear prediction, cross-faded with a raised-cosine window.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Prediction Order | `8–32 (16)` | Number of LPC coefficients used to model the signal. | Higher orders follow complex material better but can ring; lower orders smooth more. Compare on a voiced vowel. |
| Max Repair Length | `0.5–50.0 ms (3.0)` | Longest span that can be repaired. | A tiny dropout needs a short length; a longer gap needs more. If the length is too short the repair is incomplete. |

**Quick test:** create a short dropout (a click or a tiny muted gap in a test
file), order 16, length 3 ms: the gap should be filled with plausible audio
instead of a click/silence.

---

#### 28. De-Hum (`dehum`)

*Category: Noise Removal & Restoration.*

A cascade of high-Q notches at the mains frequency and its harmonics. Set the
base to 50 or 60 Hz depending on the country, then choose how many harmonics to
remove.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Base Frequency | `45–65 Hz (50)` | Mains fundamental to notch. | On a hum recording, 50 Hz removes European/Asian hum, 60 Hz removes US hum. Confirm the buzz disappears at the right setting. |
| Harmonics | `1–10 (8)` | How many multiples of the base frequency are notched. | Buzz usually needs 3–8 harmonics; at 1 only the fundamental goes and the buzzy overtones remain. Raise until the buzz is gone. |
| Notch Q | `5–40 (20)` | Width of each notch. | High Q is surgical (voice untouched); low Q removes more around each harmonic but can thin the voice. |

**Quick test:** 60 Hz hum take → base 60, harmonics 8, Q 20: buzz disappears;
set harmonics 1 and hear the remaining overtones; lower Q and hear the voice
thin.

#### 29. Plosive & Breath Suppressor (`plosive`)

*Category: Noise Removal & Restoration.*

A dynamic low-band suppressor: it detects sub-140 Hz plosive bursts relative to
mid-band voice energy and attenuates only the offending low band, plus a gentle
breath gate for unvoiced breath sounds between phrases.

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plosive Cut Sensitivity | `0–100% (60)` | How aggressively plosives are detected/attenuated. | On "Peter Piper", raise it until the thumps are gone; too high can thin normal low notes. |
| Plosive Corner | `60–220 Hz (130)` | Upper edge of the band treated as plosive. | 60–100 Hz targets only the deepest thump; 200 Hz catches more body. Keep it below the voice fundamental. |
| Breath Attenuation | `-24.0–0.0 dB (-9.0)` | How much quiet breath noise is reduced. | On a breathy speaker, −6 dB is gentle, −24 dB nearly removes breaths. At 0 dB breaths should be untouched. |

**Quick test:** read plosive-heavy text → sensitivity 60, corner 130, breath
−9 dB: "P/B" thumps soften, breaths reduce, vowels unchanged.

#### 30. De-Esser Pro (`deess`)

*Category: Noise Removal & Restoration.*

A relative sibilance suppressor with a split-band detector. **Reduction** is the
amount applied; **Center Freq** tunes the sibilant band; **Bandwidth** sets how
wide the band is; **Mode** chooses split-band (only the band is attenuated) or
broadband (the whole signal ducks).

| Control | Range (default) | What it does | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| Reduction | `0–100% (0)` | How strongly sibilance is suppressed. | 0% must be transparent. 30–60% tames "sss"; 100% can lisp. |
| Center Freq | `3500–10000 Hz (6500)` | Sibilance band center. | Sweep on "sss": the strongest reduction should occur at the hiss frequency. Female sibilance often sits higher than male. |
| Bandwidth | `10–100% (50)` | Width of the detector/attenuation band. | Low = narrow (only the hiss); high = wide (more of the consonant). Check "sh" vs "s". |
| Mode | `[Split-band \| Broadband] (Split-band)` | Split-band keeps the voice; broadband ducks the whole signal. | Split-band: only the "s" softens. Broadband: the whole word dips. Compare on "six". |

**Quick test:** "She sells seashells" → Reduction 50%, center 6.5 kHz, bandwidth
50%, split-band: hiss softens with no lisp; switch to broadband and hear the
whole word duck.
